Two inaccuracies, no puzzle impact. (1) "a word built in Greek": several were built in later languages from Greek parts — acrophobia was coined in 1887 by the Italian physician Andrea Verga (M-W: borrowed from Italian acrofobia), psychology and chronology are New/Modern Latin coinages. (2) "spelled by Greek's rules: ph for f, ch for k, y for i": onomatopoeia has none of those; its Greek mark is oe, the Latin rendering of Greek οι (Wikipedia, Romanization of Greek), which the item's own rule field already says.

Two facts check (Hesiod: Atlas holds up the heavens; Mercator's Atlas, Duisburg 1595, gave the word its map sense). But the card implies Mercator named his book after the sky-holding Titan. Mercator said he named it for Atlas "King of Mauritania, a learned philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer" (quoted by Crouch Rare Books; Wikipedia: he considered this King Atlas the first great geographer); a bibliographic note says the 1595 frontispiece shows the king, the Titan-with-globe image coming later. Britannica and M-W/Etymonline tie the usage to the Titan-on-the-frontispiece custom. Fix keeps the Titan as the visitor and states the route that all sources support.
fix_text: To the ancient Greeks, Atlas was a Titan who held up the sky. Later tellings made him a wise king of Mauretania who studied the stars. In 1595 Gerardus Mercator named his book of maps Atlas in that king's honour, and the word came to mean any book of maps.

Three problems. (1) Braid did not name hypnotism "after" the god: Etymonline says he formed it from Greek hypnos "sleep" (the word, which is also the god's name). (2) "In 1843 … named": Etymonline dates neuro-hypnotism to 1842 and hypnotism to 1843 (Braid); Wikipedia says the hypn- terms were coined by Étienne Félix d'Hénin de Cuvillers around 1820 and only popularised by Braid (that claim is flagged [citation needed] there). Sources disagree, so the card should not state the coinage as settled. (3) The rest checks: Braid was a Scottish surgeon who thought it a "nervous sleep"; Britannica says hypnosis resembles sleep only superficially; Etymonline dates hypnosis to 1850. Fix states only what every source agrees on.
fix_text: To the ancient Greeks, Hypnos was the god of sleep. In the 1840s the Scottish surgeon James Braid made the word hypnotism popular, from hypnos, the Greek word for sleep, believing it was a kind of sleep. It isn't, but the name stuck, and hypnosis followed.

fix_text: To the Norse, Frigg was queen of the gods and wife of Odin; the Anglo-Saxons called her Frige. The Roman day of Venus became her day: Friday. Freyja, a goddess of love, matches Venus more closely, and scholars still debate whether the two were once one goddess.
